content: Braxton Hicks contractions, also referred to as false labor in American English or false labour in British English, are sporadic uterine contractions that begin as early as six weeks into pregnancy. However, they are not typically felt until the second or third trimester. These contractions are sometimes called practice contractions. Braxton Hicks contractions involve a temporary tightening of the uterine muscles, lasting for about one to two minutes. They are believed to help the body prepare for childbirth. Not all pregnant individuals experience these contractions, but they are thought to play a role in the process of cervical effacement, which involves the thinning and dilation of the cervix. The term Braxton Hicks is named after Dr. John Braxton Hicks, an English physician who first described these contractions in 1872. He observed that many women experienced painless uterine contractions during the later stages of pregnancy, which often caused confusion as to whether they were entering true labor. It has since been noted that Braxton Hicks contractions are less noticeable during physical activity, unlike true labor contractions. Dehydration is considered a potential factor that can exacerbate or prolong Braxton Hicks contractions. There are several methods to alleviate Braxton Hicks contractions. These include changing positions, taking a warm bath or shower, drinking water to stay hydrated, resting, or altering one’s level of activity.
